1) in the German HNPCC cohort studied, 56% of the index patients carried a pathogenic mutation in MSH2 or MLH1, 2) 10% of the patients carried a large genomic deletion, 3) 2 mutations (MSH2, c.942+3 A>T and MLH,c.1489-1490insC) are over‐represented in the patient cohort studied, and 4) the preselection of patients by MSI

the detection rates of MMR gene mutations in HNPCC patients can be significantly raised by preselection by micro‐satellite analysis, that the spectrum of mutations is highly heterogeneous, and that a few mutations are over‐represented in the HNPCC population in Germany.
72% of tumors from HNPCC patients exhibit high MSI and 56% of index patients carry a pathogenic mutation in one of the two DNA mismatch repair genes MSH2 and/or MLH1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of the genetic disorder HNPCC, and we aim to improve genetic counseling and clinical management in HNPCC families.
the identification, analysis, and characterization of the molecular basis of hereditary non‐polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC).
the molecular genetic analysis of hereditary non‐polyposis colorectalcancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutation spectrum in HNPCC is highly variable, and that it is not possible to predict the spectrum of mutations in an individual family.
the detection rates of pathogenic mutations by screening for small mutations in MSH 2 and MLH 1 are significantly higher in patients fulfilling the AC (72% vs. 56%).
the mutation detection rate in German HNPCC families is high, and that a substantial proportion of HNPCC cases in Germany are caused by MMR gene mutations, mainly in MSH2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that a preselection by micro‐satellite analysis substantially raised the mutation detection rates in the patients who do not meet the AC.
we were able to identify a large number of novel mutations in the DNA mismatch repair genes MSH2 and Mlh1.
the detection rate of mutations in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, mainly MHS2 and MLH2, is substantially increased by microsatellite (MSI) analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the detection of mutations in MMR genes is feasible in HNPCC patients not meeting the strict Amsterdam Criteria (AC).
the mutation detection rate in HNPCC can be substantially increased by preselection of patients with MSI‐H tumors.
preselection of HNPCC families by microsatellite instability analysis substantially increases mutation detection rates.
